flags/carry-versus-overflow.asm:
Carry and overflow answer different questions

Carry asks whether the sum fitted as an unsigned number.
Overflow asks whether it fitted as a signed one. The stored bits are
the same either way, so only the reader decides which flag is the error.

     A       B  stored  CF  OF
------  ------  ------  --  --
 10000   20000   30000   0   0
 60000   10000    4464   1   0
 30000   20000   50000   0   1
 40000   40000   14464   1   1

The second row is wrong only for unsigned work and the third only for
signed work. The fourth is wrong for both, and the first for neither.
flags/direction-flag-and-strings.asm:
CLD counts up, STD counts down

source:            ABCDEFGH
copied with CLD:   ABCDEFGH
copied with STD:   ABCDEFGH

After the forward copy SI advanced to 8
After the backward copy SI retreated to 65535

The flag is global and survives a call. DOS and the BIOS assume it is clear, so a routine that sets it must clear it again.
That is why every string routine here ends with CLD, whether or not it used STD.
flags/flag-table-after-addition.asm:
Every flag after a single addition

One ADD sets all six of these, every time, whether or not the program
goes on to look at any of them. PUSHF is the way to read them without
branching on one and losing the rest.

    A      B    sum  CF  PF  AF  ZF  SF  OF
-----  -----  -----  --  --  --  --  --  --
FFFFH  0001H  0000H   1   1   1   1   0   0
7FFFH  0001H  8000H   0   1   1   0   1   1
0001H  0002H  0003H   0   1   0   0   0   0
0007H  0000H  0007H   0   0   0   0   0   0
8000H  8000H  0000H   1   1   0   1   0   1

Row one wrapped to zero and row five wrapped to zero as well, yet only
one of them overflowed as a signed sum. Row two did not carry at all and
still overflowed. No single flag tells the whole story.
flags/sign-flag-and-true-sign.asm:
When the sign flag is not the sign

The sign flag is a copy of the top bit of the stored result. When the
overflow flag is set that bit is not the sign of the true answer, and
the sign has to be read as SF exclusive or OF.

     A       B  stored  SF  OF  true sign
------  ------  ------  --  --  ---------
 20000   20000  -25536   1   1  positive
-20000  -20000   25536   0   1  negative
   100    -300    -200   1   0  negative
   300    -100     200   0   0  positive

CMP 20000 with -20000 leaves the sign set and the overflow set as well.
  JS is taken, so the sign flag alone calls 20000 the smaller.
  JL is not taken, because JL asks whether SF and OF differ.

That difference is the whole reason the signed branches exist apart from
JS and JNS. JS reads one bit and JL reads the pair.

interrupts/bios-versus-dos-output.asm:
One string, written by DOS twice and by the BIOS once

DOS 09h, whole string at once: INTEL 8086
DOS 02h, one character at a time: INTEL 8086
BIOS 0Eh teletype, one at a time: INTEL 8086

Interrupts issued: 09h once, 02h 10 times, 0Eh 10 times.

09h is one call for the whole string, so it is much the cheapest when the text is ready and dollar terminated.
02h goes through DOS, so it can be redirected to a file. 0Eh goes to the BIOS and always reaches the screen.
interrupts/interrupt-error-conventions.a:
The convention every DOS service follows

Carry clear: AX holds the result. Carry set: AX holds an error code. AX alone cannot tell you which.

Opening a file that exists:  carry clear, AX = 6
Opening one that does not:   carry set,   AX = 2
Closing a handle never open: carry set,   AX = 6

Notice that the two AX values above can be the same number. Only the carry flag separates a handle from an error.

So the test is always JC or JNC immediately after the interrupt, before anything else disturbs the flags.

utilities/leap-year-and-day-count.asm:
The leap year rule, and the day of the year
Divisible by four, except centuries, unless divisible by 400.

year   by 4  by 100  by 400  leap   days  14 June is day
1900   yes    yes    no     no     365    165
1996   yes    no     no     yes    366    166
2000   yes    yes    yes    yes    366    166
2021   no     no     no     no     365    165
2024   yes    no     no     yes    366    166
2100   yes    yes    no     no     365    165

1900 is divisible by four and by a hundred but not by four hundred, so it is not a leap year. 2000 is, because it is divisible by four hundred.
Software that tested only for divisibility by four treated 1900 and 2100 as leap years, which is where a whole class of date bugs came from.
